title: No. 16 — The Same Subject Continued (The Insufficiency of the Present Confederation to Preserve the Union) (Hamilton)
paragraphs: The tendency of the principle of legislating for States or communities in their political capacities, as shown by the experiment we have made of it, is equally confirmed by the events that have befallen all other confederate governments we know of, in exact proportion to the prevalence of that principle in those systems. The confirmation of this fact deserves a separate, detailed examination. I will only note here that of all the confederacies of antiquity that history has handed down to us, the Lycian and Achaean leagues, so far as their remains can be traced, appear to have been most free from the chains of that mistaken principle. They were accordingly the ones that have most deserved—and most generously received—the praise of political writers.

This objectionable principle may, with truth and emphasis, be called the parent of anarchy. We have seen that delinquencies on the part of the members of the Union are its natural and necessary offspring, and that whenever they happen, the only constitutional remedy is force, and the immediate effect of using force is civil war.

It remains to ask how far so hateful an instrument of government, applied to us, would even be capable of achieving its purpose. Unless a large army were constantly at the disposal of the national government, it would either not be able to use force at all or, when it could, the use would amount to a war between parts of the Confederacy over the violations of a league. In such a war, the strongest combination would most likely prevail, whether it consisted of those upholding or those resisting the general authority. It would rarely happen that the delinquency to be redressed was confined to a single member. If more than one had neglected its duty, similarity of situation would lead them to unite for common defense. Beyond this motive of sympathy, if a large and influential State happened to be the offending member, it would usually have enough weight with its neighbors to win some of them as allies. Specious arguments about danger to the common liberty could easily be devised. Plausible excuses for the offenders' deficiencies could without difficulty be invented to alarm the apprehensions, inflame the passions, and conciliate the goodwill even of States not chargeable with any violation or omission of duty. This would be all the more likely because the delinquencies of the larger members might be expected sometimes to spring from ambitious premeditation in their rulers, who hoped to throw off all external control on their schemes of personal aggrandizement. To accomplish this, they would presumably tamper beforehand with leading individuals in nearby States. If allies could not be found at home, they would turn to foreign powers, which would seldom be unwilling to encourage dissensions in a Confederacy whose firm union they had so much to fear. Once the sword is drawn, the passions of men respect no limits of moderation. The promptings of wounded pride and the urgings of irritated resentment would carry the States against which the arms of the Union were exerted to any extreme needed to avenge the affront or avoid the disgrace of submission. The first war of this kind would probably end in dissolving the Union.

This may be considered the violent death of the Confederacy. Its more natural death is what we now seem on the point of experiencing, if the federal system is not soon rebuilt in a more substantial form. Given the genius of this country, it is unlikely the complying States would often be inclined to support the authority of the Union by going to war against the non-complying States. They would always be more ready to take the milder course of putting themselves on equal footing with the delinquent members by following their example. The guilt of all would thus become the security of all. Our past experience has shown this spirit at full strength. There would in fact be an insurmountable difficulty in determining when force could properly be used. In the matter of monetary contributions, which would be the most common source of delinquency, it would often be impossible to tell whether the failure came from unwillingness or inability. The pretense of inability would always be at hand. The case would have to be very flagrant for its falseness to be detected with enough certainty to justify the harsh expedient of compulsion. It is easy to see that this problem alone, every time it arose, would open a wide field for factional motives, partiality, and oppression in whatever majority happened to prevail in the national council.

It seems to need no proof that the States ought not to prefer a national Constitution that could only be kept running through a large standing army constantly executing the ordinary requisitions or decrees of the government. Yet that is the plain alternative implied by those who deny the government the power of extending its operations to individuals. Such a scheme, if it were practical at all, would instantly degenerate into a military despotism. But in every light it will be found impractical. The resources of the Union would not suffice to maintain an army large enough to keep the larger States within the bounds of duty, nor would the means ever be available to form such an army in the first place. Anyone who considers the population and strength of several of these States singly today, and looks ahead to what they will become even half a century from now, will at once dismiss as idle and visionary any scheme aimed at regulating their movements by laws operating on them in their collective capacities and enforced by coercion applied to them in those same capacities. A project of this kind is little less fantastic than the monster-taming spirit attributed to the legendary heroes and demigods of antiquity.

Even in confederacies whose members were smaller than many of our counties, the principle of legislating for sovereign States, backed by military coercion, has never been effective. It has rarely even been attempted except against the weaker members, and in most cases attempts to coerce the refractory and disobedient have been the signals of bloody wars in which one half of the confederacy raised its banners against the other half.

The conclusion these observations must lead a thoughtful mind to is this: if it is at all possible to construct a federal government capable of regulating the common concerns and preserving the general peace, it must be founded, with regard to the objects placed under its care, on the reverse of the principle pushed by the opponents of the proposed Constitution. It must extend its action to the persons of the citizens. It must require no intermediate legislatures, but must itself be empowered to use the arm of the ordinary magistrate to enforce its own resolutions. The majesty of the national authority must be made manifest through the courts of justice. The government of the Union, like that of each State, must be able to address itself directly to the hopes and fears of individuals and to attract to its support those passions which have the strongest influence on the human heart. In short, it must possess all the means—and have the right to use all the methods—of executing the powers entrusted to it that are possessed and used by the government of the particular States.

To this reasoning it may perhaps be objected that if any State were disaffected from the authority of the Union, it could at any time obstruct the execution of its laws and bring matters to the same point of force with which the opposite scheme is reproached.

The plausibility of this objection vanishes the moment we notice the essential difference between mere NON-COMPLIANCE and DIRECT and ACTIVE RESISTANCE. If the intervention of the State legislatures is necessary to give effect to a measure of the Union, they have only NOT TO ACT, or TO ACT EVASIVELY, and the measure is defeated. This neglect of duty can be disguised under feigned but flimsy provisions, so as not to appear, and so not to alarm the people about the safety of the Constitution. State leaders may even take credit for their stealthy invasions of it on the ground of some temporary convenience, exemption, or advantage.

But if the execution of the laws of the national government did not require the intervention of the State legislatures—if those laws operated immediately on the citizens themselves—the particular governments could not interrupt their progress without an open and violent exertion of an unconstitutional power. No omissions or evasions would suffice. They would be obliged to act, and to act in a way that would leave no doubt that they had encroached on national rights. An experiment of this nature would always be hazardous in the face of a constitution at all capable of defending itself, and of a people enlightened enough to distinguish between a legal exercise and an illegal usurpation of authority. Success would require not merely a factious majority in the legislature, but the cooperation of the courts of justice and of the body of the people. If the judges were not in conspiracy with the legislature, they would declare the resolutions of such a majority contrary to the supreme law of the land, unconstitutional, and void. If the people were not infected with the spirit of their State representatives, they—as the natural guardians of the Constitution—would throw their weight onto the national side and give it a decided edge in the contest. Attempts of this kind would not often be made lightly or rashly, because they could seldom be made without danger to those who made them, except in cases of tyrannical exercise of federal authority.

If opposition to the national government were to arise from the disorderly conduct of refractory or seditious individuals, it could be put down by the same means used daily against the same evil under the State governments. The magistracy, being equally the ministers of the law of the land—whatever its source—would no doubt be as ready to guard national regulations as local ones from the inroads of private lawlessness. As for the partial commotions and insurrections that sometimes disturb society, springing from the intrigues of a small faction or from sudden or occasional ill-humors that do not infect the body of the community, the general government could draw on more extensive resources to suppress them than any single member could. As for those mortal feuds that, in certain circumstances, spread a conflagration through a whole nation or a very large portion of it—proceeding either from weighty grievances created by the government or from the contagion of some violent popular paroxysm—they fall outside any ordinary calculation. When they happen, they usually amount to revolutions and dismemberments of empire. No form of government can always avoid or control them. It is vain to hope to guard against events too mighty for human foresight or precaution, and idle to object to a government because it cannot perform impossibilities.
